---
title: The model as data
jupyter: python3
---

A disease written as code, as a class whose `step()` method changes arrays of agents, can be run but not read: Starsim can't describe the model, draw it, or run it any other way. A *declared* disease is instead a set of objects (states, transitions, parameters) that describe the model without running it. Everything else is derived from them: the description, the diagram and equations, the stratified model, the run's hash, the saved spec, and the engines that run it as an ODE, a stochastic compartmental model, or agents.

This page covers those objects, what Starsim does with them when a module is built, and how it fills in what you left out. [From model to run](build_and_run.qmd) covers what happens next.

## States and transitions

A **state** (`ss.State`) is something a person can be in: a compartment in an ODE, a boolean array over agents in an agent-based run. A **transition** (`ss.Transition`) moves people between states, driven by a rate, a dwell time, a branch probability, or a trigger. There are three ways to write a model, and they build the same objects:

```python
import starsim as ss

# Operators: "S goes to I at rate beta times I"
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10),
)

# Fully explicit, e.g. for building models in a loop or from another language
S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(
    ss.Transition(S, I, rate=0.3 * I, name='infection'),
    ss.Transition(I, R, dur=ss.days(10), name='recovery'),
)

# A class, when there is also behavior that isn't a transition
class SIR(ss.Disease):
    S, I, R   = ss.states('S I R')
    infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)
```

All three give the same model hash (`sim.hash().model`). This is a rule of the design: a keyword means the same thing in every form, and subclassing adds behavior, not vocabulary. A transition takes the state objects themselves, never their names as strings, so nothing is inferred from a name.

## Rates are expressions

When you write `0.3 * I`, nothing is computed. `I` is a state, so the result is an expression: a small tree whose leaves are parameters, states, counts (`I.n`), and properties of people (`ss.ppl.age`), joined by arithmetic and NumPy functions. Each engine evaluates the same tree in its own terms: a value for each group of a compartmental model, for each agent, or as JAX arrays so a gradient can be taken through the run. This is what lets a model written once be run by any solver.

Two kinds of leaf differ. **`I.n`** is the number of people in `I`, used literally. A **bare `I`** means contact with people in `I`: with no network that's `I.n / N`, so `beta * I` is the textbook `beta * S * I / N`, and with a network each engine works it out from who actually meets whom, which no single formula can say. Since that is a sum over contacts, a rate must be linear in its bare states (`beta * I * I` raises a `ValueError`).

The **kind** of a transition is derived from its rate, not declared: if the rate mentions a bare state, the transition is contact-mediated and that state is a source of infection; otherwise it is spontaneous. You can see this on the transition itself:

```python
sir.infection.contact     # True: its rate mentions I
sir.infection.terms       # {I: par(0.3)}: the coefficient of each source of infection
sir.recovery.contact      # False
```

## Parameters

A number written inline becomes a parameter of the module, named after its slot: above, `sir.pars` has `beta` (the coefficient of `I`) and `dur` (the dwell time of recovery), qualified by the transition if two would clash (`dur_recovery`). Wrap a value in `ss.par()` when it needs a name, bounds, or a source; bounds are what make it fittable, since `sim.fit()` fits every parameter with bounds to every result with data. A value may also vary by group (`ss.by(age=[...])`), in time (`ss.timeseries()`), or between people (a distribution): the slot decides what a value means, and the form is free. Setting a parameter the module doesn't have raises a `KeyError`, since a misspelling that is silently ignored is one of the hardest bugs to find. See [Parameters](../user_guide/models_parameters.qmd).

## Dimensions

Age, sex, place, and risk group are all handled by one operation, `stratify()`, which takes a finished model and divides it by a property of people:

```python
sim = ss.Sim(sir, stratify=dict(age=[0, 15, 65]))   # or sim.stratify(age=...), for every module
sir.stratify(risk=['low', 'high'], adjust={'infection': [1, 3]})  # one disease's own dimension
```

Stratifying doesn't copy the states: `sir` still has `S`, `I`, and `R`, and the dimension becomes an axis. In a compartmental run each state has one row per group; as agents the property is an array on the people, and the groups are used for adjustments, conditions, and results. The base model and the stratification don't refer to each other, which is what lets one disease be reused with different structures. A stratified result is still one result (`res.I.select(age='0-14')`, `res.I.by('age')`). Properties of people are normally stratified on the sim, because every disease has to agree on them.

## The graph: resolve, complete, check

When `ss.Disease(...)` is called, it builds the module's graph (`ss.graph.Graph`, in `starsim/internals/graph.py`). The graph is where the objects you wrote become a model:

1. **Collect and name.** It gathers the states, transitions, parameters, and results, and names any that have no name: from the keyword they were passed under, then a `name=` argument, then the variable they're bound to in the calling code. A transition with none of these gets a name built from its endpoints (`S_to_I`); a state with none raises a `ValueError`, since a made-up state name would leak into results.
2. **Resolve.** It finds which states are people and which are plain counts (a water reservoir, a mosquito population), derives the kind of each transition from its rate, marks the sources of infection, works out which transitions are acquisitions of the disease, and finds the first state (where people start and are born into).
3. **Complete.** It turns inline values into named parameters, and groups the exits of each state into those that compete (rates, resolved together in one draw, so declaration order never matters) and those that split on entry (`p=`).
4. **Check.** It checks what can be checked without a sim: the time dimension of every rate, that branch probabilities add up, that exposure is linear, and that keywords name real parameters.

So mistakes in the model's structure are errors when the disease is built, at the line that made it. What needs the sim (the unit of bare numbers, values against their bounds, the shapes of values by group, the choice of solver) is checked at `sim.init()`.

Picking names up from variables is convenient but implicit, so it happens in one place, once. It can miss (a transition written inline in the call gets the fallback name), and `describe()` shows the names used.

## Guessed defaults

Short models leave a lot unsaid: how a dwell time is distributed, how people mix, how many there are. Starsim fills each gap with a default and records the rule that produced it: a **guessed default**. `describe()` prints the resolved model with every guess marked, so nothing is assumed silently:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
beta = ss.par(bounds=[0.1, 1.0], source='to be fitted')
sir = ss.Disease(
    infection = S >> I @ beta * I,
    recovery  = I >> R @ ss.lognorm_ex(mean=ss.days(10), std=ss.days(3)),
    init_prev = 0.01,
)
sim = ss.Sim(sir, stop=100)
sim.describe()
```

Every `[guessed: ...]` is a choice you didn't make: 10,000 people, the ODE solver, homogeneous mixing, 11 Erlang stages for the lognormal dwell time, and `beta` starting at the geometric middle of its bounds. Each guess is tested both ways: a model that makes it has it marked, and one that doesn't, doesn't.

Because the model is data, its other views come for free:

```{python}
sir.equations()
sir.transitions
```

`sir.diagram()` gives the same graph as a Mermaid flowchart, and `sim.to_spec()` as JSON (see [The model spec, errors, and interop](spec_and_interop.qmd)).

## Limits

- **Code is opaque.** A function given as a rate (`rate=my_fn`) isn't analyzed in advance; if it needs something only agents have, a compartmental run stops and says what it asked for.
- **A disease written as code is not data.** A disease with its own `define_states()` and `step()` runs as agents in the same loop, but `describe()` shows only its class, arrays, and parameters. A class can mix the two: declared transitions, plus code in `step()` after `super().step()`.
- **Some things need agents.** A distribution across people or an individual-level network has no compartmental form, so `solver='auto'` runs the model as agents and says why. See [Solvers](solvers.qmd).
